memories.memory_text: I was in the bath, just trying to clean off the day, watching Bilko in the mirror—then suddenly a man in uniform blocked the screen, and I couldn't see his face, just his body looming there. I froze, heart pounding, and all I could get out was 'Who's there?'

I saw Spencer Keaton burst out and run toward the burning car, then I came roaring around the corner in the Stonebridge Station—he spotted me and started chasing after it, shouting something desperate.
Later, I heard that Owen Winslow—Blair Hale’s daughter—told Spencer Keaton my name, though I wasn’t there when it happened.
They know my name, my face, my body—I can feel it spreading, like ink in water. If they’ve reached the records, they’ve seen everything: the scar, the blemish, the weight of me reduced to numbers.

I stood at the Sawyer Rivers's the weathered photograph demanding he re-stamp my form—he'd done it before, so why not now? His refusal made my skin crawl, like the system was tightening around me again.
I slammed my fist on the the weathered photograph and told Sawyer Rivers those weren't tits—he was looking at twenty pounds of high explosive, and I'd blow the place up if he didn't stamp the form.

I was just standing there with the form when suddenly armed Lakeside Department burst out of secret doors, shouting 'DROP IT!!'—I dropped it right away, hands up, heart pounding. I couldn't believe they were treating me like a threat.

Spencer Keaton rushed in and shouted 'STOP! Let her go!'—then the Lakeside Department snapped to attention when they saw his badge. I didn't understand what was happening, but he grabbed me and pulled me away, saying it was a classified matter.
I was already pulling away in the Stonebridge Station when I saw Spencer Keaton sprinting toward me, jumping onto the running board—he barely made it inside.
I stared at him, engine off, and demanded to know who he was—no way was I driving blind with some panicked man babbling about dreams and danger.
After he dropped papers all over my cab, I told him straight—'Don't litter my cab!'—and watched him scramble to pick them up like he finally remembered I was in charge here.
I told Spencer Keaton to shut up about his dreams—I don’t care what he thinks or feels. It’s my life, not his.
I asked Spencer Keaton where he was taking me, then realized—no, I’m the one driving. I’m in control now.
I told Spencer Keaton not to act guilty, to act like me—just doing the job—because I could see he was poking around, getting too curious for his own good.
When the Stonebridge Station stopped, I reached behind the seat and took the package, quickly slipping it under my jacket while checking that Spencer Keaton wasn’t looking.
I moved toward the corner of the metal structure, keeping low, scanning for watchers—there was no time to hesitate, not with the the brass letter burning a hole in my hands.
We passed the parcels—mine to them, theirs to me—fast, no words, just a shift of weight and a glance toward the Ministry poster that felt like it was watching us.
I turned the key and felt the engine roar to life under my hands, the the brass letter wedged behind me like a silent passenger, Spencer Keaton’s eyes burning into my neck as we pulled away.

I told him it was a Christmas present, and when he picked it up and gave me that look, I just said, 'Open it if you don't trust me,' like I didn't care—but I watched him, waiting to see if he'd actually do it.
I pushed Spencer Keaton on what Silverline Holdings really does, how it claims to fight terrorists but ends up destroying innocent lives like the Buttles'.
I threw out that line about wars having innocent victims, then hit him with 'Who is this war against, Spencer Keaton?'—watching him fumble for an answer that wasn’t there.
I saw the clock as we passed it—right on time, just like always. I said it out loud, maybe to steady myself, knowing I had to punch in by five.

Spencer Keaton lunged for the wheel—I shoved him back, but he kept grabbing, trying to force a turn. I couldn't control the Stonebridge Station while he was tearing at the steering wheel, screaming at me to stop.
I was fighting Spencer Keaton for control of the Stonebridge Station, screaming that he was mad, completely out of his mind—then the sirens ripped through the air and we both turned to look.
I grabbed for control of the Stonebridge Station, shouting at Spencer Keaton to stop—we can't outrun them, he's going to get us killed.
I shouted at Spencer Keaton not to touch the gear levers while we were fighting for control of the Stonebridge Station, the Harbor Point Police closing in behind us.
I felt Spencer Keaton shove my hand away and then that awful jolt when the trailer ripped loose from the cab—I knew right then we were in real trouble.
I snapped at Spencer Keaton, 'We? Don't blame me!'—I couldn't let him pin this on us like we were in it together.
I saw the house burning behind us and shouted 'Shit! The house is on fire!'—then I had to snap Spencer Keaton out of it, tapping his forehead, telling him to come back.

Spencer Keaton grabbed the the brass letter from the trolley like he had any right to it—like he didn’t already ruin everything. I lunged for it, heart slamming, because that thing wasn’t his to touch.

Spencer Keaton grabbed the the brass letter I was carrying—the one from the power plant. I didn’t throw it at him. We were in the lingerie department when he started questioning me, then lunged for it.
I asked Noel Mercer if he repeats everything, and he just nodded, confirming it like it was nothing—his voice flat, echoing Sasha Finch’s words like a broken machine.
The Sawyer Rivers looked me up and down and asked if I was a professional—like I was some kind of threat or fraud—and I just said, 'No, amateur,' like it was obvious.

memories.memory_text: I cut them down—one after another—the robed figures falling like shadows under my blade, their bodies piling up in a heap of black cloth while I barely got a scratch.
The pile of black shapes began to rise, turning into a churning cloud of flapping cloth. It lifted off the ground and flew away, emitting a terrifying maniacal laughter.
I had her—she was right there in the cage, and I told her she was safe, that no one could ever reach us up on that platform surrounded by all those eyes watching the sky.

The sky started cracking like glass, then whole blocks of it were ripped out, one by one, until everything went black—and then I saw that flapping black shape coming at me, and I couldn’t move fast enough.

I saw the the silver radio Skyler Huxley handed me and realized it was meant for Spencer Huxley—but he’d already panicked, correcting himself, saying it was Blair Hale. I could feel the weight of it, like it was something dangerous just to hold.
I sat at the console and started checking the system—Blair Hale was flagged everywhere as gone: dormanted, deleted, inoperative. I remember thinking, he’s not just missing—he’s been erased.
I burst into Alex Marlowe's flat and saw a hole in the floor—everything looked abandoned, like she’d been ripped out of here suddenly.
I heard an explosion, ran to the window, and saw my car on fire—Alex Marlowe was running across the forecourt with a suitcase and bundles, getting away fast.
I punched in Alex Marlowe’s name and pulled up her file—Suspect S/5173, truck Alex Marlowe, all inquiries to Room 5001. That’s what I needed.
I was running full speed toward the Stonebridge Station as it started moving, and I barely managed to leap onto the running board and haul myself up into the cab.

I found the luggage Alex Marlowe had taken from the apartment hidden behind the seats in the Stonebridge Station—same pieces she carried away, now crammed in with rags and grease. My sleeve got dirty when I opened the compartment, and I was still checking them when the door suddenly flew open.

I saw her pull a package from behind the seat, look around quickly, and slide it under her jacket before walking off. I didn’t see what it was—just the way she moved, furtive, like she didn’t want me to know.

I begged Rowan Reeves to help me check if Alex Marlowe had been arrested, but he shut me down, saying she was involved in blowing up Harbor Point Police men and linked to Spencer Huxley’s sabotage—then just left me standing there.
I remember stepping out of the Fairview Hospital with Rowan Reeves, desperate to make him understand—Alex Marlowe was innocent—but instead of helping, he just asked me to stay away from him.

I walked in and my breath turned to steam—everything was torn open, frozen, like my apartment had been gutted and left to die. When I asked what happened, they just said 'Thermostat's gone. And then some,' like that explained the wreckage.

I told Alex Marlowe I’d be back soon and not to answer the phone or the door—she looked worried, and when she said 'Don’t do anything silly,' I could hear the fear in her voice, but I had to go. I’m going to pull some strings at the Ministry, even if it’s dangerous, because it’s the only way to fix this mess and keep her safe.

I saw my Darian Marlowe's picture sitting on Quinn Vale's the weathered photograph—just there, out in the open, like it was normal. I didn't understand why it was in his Silverbrook Park, of all places.
The machine printed that Trollope was dead—'resisting arrest'—but no arrest was ever logged. I watched the message come through twice, and then I turned the system back on. Something was very wrong.
I opened the door and saw her—dancing in that glowing light, wearing my Darian Marlowe’s wig, floating like Owen Winslow from my dreams. I couldn’t speak. It was her, but it couldn’t be.
She looked at me after reading the print-out and said, 'Care for a bit of necrophilia?'—and then we rushed together. I don’t know if it was real, but I felt it.
I soared up into that brilliant blue sky, my wings catching the light—I could see the clouds rushing, and for the first moment, I knew I had found the day.
I drove my sword into the column with everything I had—the crack split upward, and when the cube shattered, the sky burst free and the Harper Finch' chains fell away.

I woke up and saw the light on the wall, and for a moment I smiled—I remembered where I was, and I reached for Alex Marlowe. She wasn't there, and I panicked—then she said 'Merry Xmas' and crawled back to me. I held her and said, 'Everything is going to be all right.'

There was a crash—something tore through the ceiling like a drill. Lakeside Department slid down a pole, grabbed me, called me 'Turncoat Bastard' and 'Traitor.' A bag was pulled over my head, and just before everything went black, I heard a shot and Alex Marlowe screamed.

I screamed for Rowan Reeves, begging him to stop—he was coming at me with that thing, mask half off, shouting it was a professional relationship, but his voice was breaking like he didn’t believe it either.

The ceiling exploded open and Spencer Huxley dropped through with armed men behind him—guns firing, Rowan Reeves falling, then the room shaking from an explosion right after Spencer Huxley yelled 'Detonate!' and started unstrapping me.
I was running down those endless stairs, fighting, bleeding, shots ringing out all around me—I don’t even know who was left, just that I had to keep moving.
Spencer Huxley threw me a dark overcoat, and I pulled it on fast to hide my light grey detainee clothes.
We burst through the door together, running into the open forecourt while gunfire echoed behind us.
I saw the building explode—huge bursts of fire and debris everywhere, and all those files just tearing out into the sky like snow, fluttering down over everything.
I turned to find Spencer Huxley after the blast, but he was gone—completely gone—and then I heard gunfire closing in, so I ran.
I burst into the flat and ran straight to the bedroom—everything was gone, just empty walls and curtains blowing in the wind. I couldn’t find any sign she’d ever been there.
I was trapped at the end of the maze, digging through that pile of broken machines—televisions, washers, junk everywhere—just trying to find something to defend myself as the agents closed in.
My hand brushed against a door knob as I pressed against the wall—turned it, and the door just opened. I didn't think, I just dove through.
I saw the Alex Marlowe’s head in the mirror, wearing Alex Marlowe’s cap, and when she looked up and smiled, I knew it was her—alive, real, here for me. I couldn’t hold it back, I just sobbed.
I woke up and saw her come through the door, and when she asked if I slept well, I just nodded and said it quietly—'I don't dream anymore'—before pulling her close.

I'm sitting in the chair, strapped in, but I can't feel the restraints anymore—just the warmth of the sky opening up around me, and my humming rising into something grander, like an orchestra answering me.
I see Quinn Vale and someone else turn away, their backs receding—Rowan Reeves said 'He's gone'—and I know they think I'm lost, but I'm not gone, I'm finally here, finally free, singing into the sky.
